items.note: The Udaipur inscription records a land donation in the presence of the deity Udalmēśvara, 'evidently Udayeśvara', installed in the temple; donee unnamed so the gift was to the deity; donor Dhāmadēya, treasury officer of king Dēvapāla.
Opens with siddham; year 1286 in numerals, Vikrama era, equal to 1229 A.C. (northern expired); Friday in bright Kārttika, corresponding to 26 October or 2 November.
Editor says the donated village was probably near Udaipur and suggests Udaipur itself may be meant by the expression Pañchamukhapattana (Pañchamukha taken as Śiva).
Dēvapāla is identical with the Paramāra ruler of Dhārā, whose earliest known date is Harsūd VS 1275 and another is the Māndhātā grant of VS 1282.
Footnote: by the Kārttikādi Vikrama reckoning the Friday of bright Kārttika fell on 11 or 18 October 1230 A.C.
Footnote on the reading 'visvē' in line 12, possibly connected with the local word for the 20th part of a bighā (Visvā, perhaps a corrupt vimśātika).

Second Udaipur record in Dēvapāla's reign, donating plots of land in villages; one village appears to be Dēvadharmapurī, 'probably Udaipur itself'; dated Thursday, third of dark Mārgaśīrsha, year 1289 (unit figure indistinct).

claim.value: two Dēvapāla-period records (VS 1286 and 1289) at Udaipur in this edition

items.note: Date corresponds to 2 December 123[2] A.C., found at the same place as the record dated three years earlier; the latest known epigraph of Dēvapāla's time.

Muslim sources say Dēvapāla was alive in 1233-34 when Sultān Iltutmish raided Mālwā, captured Bhilsā and demolished the Mahākāla temple at Ujjain; later Dēvapāla's son's grant says he killed a Muslim governor at Bhilsā; Paramāra possession continued in 1263 and 1269.
refs: Elliot, Hist. of India, Vol. II, p. 328

items.note: The record gives Dēvapāla the paramount titles Paramabhaṭṭāraka and Mahārājādhirāja; the editor calls it the only epigraphic evidence claiming imperial titles for him.
Bhriṅgāri is the same as Bhriṅgārīkā in a record from the same place of a village grant by Lūṇapasāka to god Vaidyanātha in 1173 A.C.; modern Bhiraṅgāvalī about 6 km north-east of Udaipur.
Dēvadharmapurī, if the reading is correct, seems to be the village of Udaipur itself.
Pañchamukha-pattana is taken as the town or village named after the Śiva temple, i.e. Nīlakaṇṭheśvara, at Udaipur itself; one place with two names, 'rather curious'.
Village Kharahi may be Khiriyā or Khadākhēdī, about 6 km north-west of Udaipur; Umarata is modern Umarathā nearby.
